correct_answer: A compound in smoke, not fire's heat, tells some seeds that open ground has arrived

passage:
A wildfire leaves behind what looks like an ending: black ground, ash, the smell of smoke for weeks. For a number of plant families, particularly in South Africa and Australia, it is closer to a starting gun. Seeds that have lain in the soil for years, sometimes for decades, germinate within a season of a burn, and they do so in numbers that bare ground alone never produces.

For most of the last century the explanation on offer was heat. Fire warms the upper soil, and warmth cracks hard seed coats; that much is true, and for certain species it is the whole story. But it did not cover the many seeds that responded to fires whose heat never reached them, or the gardeners who found that smoke blown across a seed tray worked as well as a flame. In the 1990s researchers began filtering smoke through water and pouring the water onto seeds. The seeds germinated. Something carried in the smoke, and not the heat, was the signal.

The active compounds, later named karrikins, form when cellulose burns. They are stable in soil, active at vanishingly small concentrations, and they act on the same internal machinery that holds a seed dormant. A dormant seed is not asleep so much as held: its growth is checked by hormones that must be overruled before a root will emerge. Karrikins tip that balance.

What makes the signal worth obeying is its honesty. Warmth can arrive in any spring; a burst of light can arrive when a single branch falls. Smoke from burning plant matter arrives only after fire has stripped the canopy and returned a flush of nutrients to the soil, in the one week of a decade when a seedling has light, minerals, and no neighbors. The seed is not detecting fire. It is detecting the brief, uncrowded ground that fire leaves behind.

passage:
In 1806 a young Bostonian named Frederic Tudor loaded a brig with blocks cut from a pond on his family's farm and sailed for Martinique. The cargo was ice. Insurers refused the risk, sailors thought the hold would flood, and the city's shipping columns printed the departure as a curiosity. Tudor lost money on that voyage and on nearly every voyage he attempted for the next fifteen years, twice going to debtors' prison. What defeated him was not melting at sea, which proved slower than anyone had predicted, but melting on shore: a cargo that survived the crossing sat in rented warehouses and was gone within weeks.

The remedy, when it came, was not a better ship. It was sawdust. Tudor found that the waste of Maine's lumber mills, packed around the blocks, held cold better than the hay and straw that had been standard, and cost nothing because the mills were glad to be rid of it. Around the same time his supplier Nathaniel Wyeth devised a horse-drawn cutter that scored the surface of a frozen pond into a grid, so that uniform blocks could be broken out and stacked without gaps. Hand-sawn ice had come in wedges and rounds that left air between them; Wyeth's blocks fit like masonry, and air was the enemy.

By the 1850s ice from New England ponds was arriving in Calcutta, Rio de Janeiro, and Hong Kong, and Tudor, who had been a figure of local ridicule, died wealthy. Yet the trade's foundation was always seasonal and local, and it did not survive the arrival of mechanical refrigeration; by 1900 the ponds were quiet. The industry that had made cold into cargo lasted less than a century, and its most durable legacy was a habit of mind: the expectation, now unremarkable, that a perishable thing might travel.

The wall along my grandfather's north field fell down every winter, and every June we put it up again. I was nine the first summer he let me help, and I understood the job as a race. I could carry two stones to his one. I set them where they looked right and moved on, and by noon I had laid twice his length of wall, and by August most of my length had slumped into the grass.

Nobody built that wall on purpose, he told me. Farmers in that county had not gone looking for stone; the stone had come up out of the ground, pushed to the surface each spring by frost, and had to be put somewhere that was not the plow's path. So the walls were less structures than heaps of a nuisance, arranged. What frost delivered, frost took back. It was, he said, a conversation with the winter, and the winter always got the last word.

He worked slowly because he was not lifting stones, he was reading them. He would pick one up, turn it, feel for the flat that wanted to face down, and often set it aside entirely for a stone that was uglier and fit better. I chose by the face; he chose by the bottom. My wall stood until the first rain found the gaps I had left; his stood until frost, which is to say, as long as anything there stood.

I have not put up a wall in twenty years. But I notice that I have stopped trusting the parts of my work that look finished soonest, and that when something I have made comes apart I am less surprised than I used to be, and less insulted. The wall taught me that badly, over several summers, and I am still not sure I have it right.

By half past five the shutters were down, though no one in Fenwick Street would want a watch mended before eight. Ada Verrell liked the hour for its emptiness: the long counter still cold, the brass weights sleeping in their velvet trays, the forty clocks on the wall keeping forty slightly different opinions of the time. He had been dead eleven months. In that time the trade had not so much left her as circled her at a distance, the way water circles a stone. Men who had brought him their repeaters for thirty years now carried them past her window to Leeming's in the market square, and came back a fortnight later to say, with a kind of apology in the shoulders, that Leeming had not quite got it. "Thursday is soon," Ada said.

The balance staff was broken; it was three hours' work, and she could have named the fault from the doorway. She named nothing. She wrote the ticket, gave him the stub, told him Friday, and when the door had shut she allowed herself the smallest possible smile — and then took up the tweezers, because the smile did not mend anything.

For most of the last century, a sociologist who wanted to know whether a neighborhood was trusting did the sensible thing and asked. Surveys went door to door carrying a question in some version of this one: would you say that most people around here can be trusted? The answers were tabulated, mapped, and compared across cities, and for decades they stood as the discipline's best evidence about the texture of civic life.

The trouble is that answering a survey costs nothing. A resident who has never lent a ladder in her life can still say yes, and a resident who watches four children who are not hers may say no because the week has been long. What the survey records is a person's account of a neighborhood, delivered to a stranger with a clipboard, and an account is not a behavior.

So a handful of researchers stopped asking and started leaving things on the ground. In the lost-letter technique, a team scatters stamped, addressed envelopes across a district and then waits by the mailbox at the other end. Nobody is interviewed. Nothing is claimed. The measure is the return rate: the proportion of strangers who picked up mail that was not theirs and carried it far enough to post it.

The elegance of the design is also its weakness. A high return rate may reflect neighborly feeling, or it may reflect a mailbox on every second corner and a population that walks past them. Rain suppresses returns. So does a block where the sidewalk belongs mainly to people hurrying for a bus.

What has proved most useful is not either number but the gap between them. Districts that describe themselves as close-knit sometimes return the fewest letters, and districts that shrug at the clipboard sometimes return the most. Where the two measures diverge, something in the neighborhood is worth going back to look at.

He was at the finisher with a boot on the last and the belt running, which in this shop had always been the same thing as saying he was not available.

The harbour empties twice a day, and for two hours around low water it is not a harbour at all but a field of grey mud with boats lying in it. The dinghies go over on their sides, keels showing, ropes slack from the wall. Gulls walk out where at noon there were four fathoms. Visitors who arrive at the wrong hour take one photograph and leave, having seen, they think, a place in decline.

They have seen only the interval. The mud is the harbour's working capital: it is what the water has left behind, ton upon ton of it, and every spring the men come down with the dredger and take some of it away, and every winter the burn brings more. The wall itself was built in 1841 from stone quarried a mile inland, and it has been rebuilt in three places since, each repair a slightly different colour, so that the whole structure reads like a page with corrections in the margin.

At half-flood the change begins. Water comes in over the mud in a thin sheet, silently, without any of the drama a stranger expects; there is no wave, no announcement. The dinghies stir, lift, and are level again within the hour, and by evening the harbour looks exactly as the postcards have it — blue, brimming, tidy. Nothing has been restored. passage:
A bell is not tuned when it is cast; it is tuned afterward, by being made lighter. The founder deliberately pours a shape he knows will sound wrong, and it leaves the mould sharp — above the note wanted — because bronze can be cut away and cannot be put back.

A struck bell does not give one note. It gives at least five, sounding together from different points on the rim and waist, and the ear hears a single voice only because the founder has forced them into a fixed relationship: hum, prime, tierce, quint, nominal. If the tierce drifts, the bell is not slightly wrong; it is a different instrument, sour in a way that listeners who could not name the interval will hear from the churchyard.

The tuning is done on a vertical lathe. The bell is set mouth upward, and a cutter shaves bronze from the inside — a few thousandths of an inch, then a strike, then a reading. Each partial answers to a different band of the interior wall, so metal taken from one band lowers one partial and leaves its neighbours nearly untouched. The skill lies in the order. Correcting the nominal first can put the tierce beyond recovery, since every cut is permanent and there is no way to give the metal back.

Before 1900 this work was done largely by ear, and English founders in particular tuned the nominal only, letting the other partials fall where the casting had put them. The results were serviceable, and many of them are still ringing. What changed after 1900 was measurement, not hearing. Once a tuner could watch the partials on a meter he could hold five of them at once, and the cleanness of the modern bell dates from that instrument rather than from any new alloy or any sharpening of the human ear.

By the middle of the eighteenth century a Londoner walking east from Temple Bar could read the walls of the houses. Fixed high above the doors, out of the reach of thieves, were small lead plaques bearing a sun, a phoenix, or a pair of clasped hands, each with a number stamped beneath it. These were firemarks, and they announced that the householder had insured with one office or another and had paid his premium for the year.

The offices had not set out to fight fires. The Sun, founded in 1710, and its rivals were businesses that sold policies, and the brigades they eventually maintained were an expense grudgingly accepted. It was cheaper to keep a crew of watermen in livery, with an engine and a cart, than to pay out on a house that burned to the cellar. The brigades were instruments of accounting before they were instruments of rescue, and the firemark was less a badge of protection than a receipt.

What followed has often been told as farce: rival crews racing to a blaze, finding the wrong mark on the wall, and standing by while the building burned. The record is more sober. Crews did reach uninsured houses and did sometimes work them, partly because a fire left alone would spread to houses that were insured, and partly because the men were paid gratuities by grateful neighbors. The system's real defect was quieter than any race. Each office covered the districts where its own policies were thick, so protection followed wealth street by street, and the poorest parishes, where houses stood closest together and fires began most often, were served worst.

The remedy, when it came in 1833, was not a public service. Ten of the offices merged their brigades into a single London Fire Engine Establishment under one superintendent, still paid for out of premiums. James Braidwood, brought down from Edinburgh to command it, trained his men to enter burning buildings rather than to play water on them from the street, and the Establishment answered calls whatever plaque hung on the wall. Yet it remained a private body, and its officers said plainly that they existed to limit the losses of their subscribers. When Parliament at last created a public brigade in 1865, the argument that carried the day was not that the insurers had failed to save lives but that they had never been asked to.

The bus set me down at the foot of the hill, and I walked the last mile to my uncle's orchard as I had every August since I was seven. The road had been resurfaced. Everything else had the worn, exact look of a place that has been kept rather than improved: the gate still swung a hand's width short of its post, and you still had to lift it.

My uncle Tobias was in the third row with a knife and a roll of tape, doing what he called his winter work in the wrong season. He grafted. He would cut a slip from one tree, set it into the wound of another, bind the two together and walk away, and eleven months later there would be an argument settled somewhere inside the bark. He had never explained any of this to me when I was a child. He had handed me the tape.

My father, his brother, had sold his own share of the orchard the year I was born and had never once, in my hearing, regretted it. He was a man who liked a finished thing. He could build a shelf in an afternoon and sit looking at it in the evening; if he could not see the end of a job from its beginning, he did not begin. Tobias could not see the end of anything he did, and began everything.

"You've come at a bad time," Tobias said, without looking up. "The Ashmead is failing."

I said I was sorry.

"Don't be. It's ninety years old. Nothing here is failing that isn't also doing something else." He held up a slip of green wood between two fingers. "This is off it."

I understood then, more slowly than I like to admit, what he had been doing through all those Augusts. The orchard was not a collection of trees. It was one long argument he was carrying forward on behalf of people who had planted before he was born, and the trees were only its sentences. A sentence could fail and the argument go on.

He gave me the knife. I made the cut badly, too shallow, and he did not take the knife back. He turned the slip a quarter turn in my hand, said "Again," and went off down the row to look at something else, leaving me there among ninety years of somebody's patience with my thumb bleeding lightly onto the tape.

A piano tuner spends the afternoon making a piano slightly wrong. This is not carelessness; it is the only way the instrument can be made to work at all. The trouble lies in arithmetic. Tune a series of perfect fifths upward from a low note, twelve of them in succession, and you ought to arrive back at the note you began with, seven octaves higher. You do not. The note you reach is a shade too high, by a discrepancy small enough to be dismissed on paper and impossible to ignore in a room. Somewhere the excess must be absorbed.

Different centuries absorbed it differently. Early keyboard tunings dumped nearly the whole error into a few intervals, leaving most of the instrument gloriously pure and a handful of chords unusable; players called the worst of them a wolf, for the howl it produced. Later tunings spread the error more widely but never evenly, so that every key kept a flavour of its own: D major bright and faintly strained, E-flat major broad and settled. When eighteenth-century writers insisted that keys had characters, they were not being fanciful.

Equal temperament, which came to dominate the nineteenth century, took the opposite route. It divides the error into twelve identical portions and gives every interval the same slight impurity. Nothing is pure; nothing is unusable. A composer could modulate into any key at all and find it waiting, sounding exactly like every other key transposed. The gain was mobility. The cost, less often mentioned, was that the individual colours drained away.

What a tuner hears while doing this is not pitch but beats. When two notes are close but not identical, their sound waves reinforce and cancel in a slow pulsation, a wavering in the tone that can be counted against a watch. The tuner does not listen for a chord that sounds right; he listens for a wavering that arrives at the correct speed, six a second here, four there, and sets the string when the count matches.

A violinist need not accept any of this. Playing a phrase, she can bend a third slightly narrow to make it ring, adjusting from bar to bar as the harmony demands; singers do the same without being taught. The pianist has no such freedom. Every compromise in the instrument was settled before she sat down, by somebody else, in the afternoon, with a wrench and a watch. She inherits a set of decisions and plays as though they were natural law, which, for the length of the concert, they are.

Ask where a forest stores its carbon and most people will point at the trunks. It is a reasonable guess and a partial one. Across the world's temperate and boreal forests, more carbon is held in the soil than in all the wood, leaves, and roots standing above it; in many stands, two or three times as much. The visible forest is the smaller half of the account.

Soil acquires its share by a slower route than the trunk does. A tree draws carbon dioxide from the air and builds it into wood, but it also leaks a substantial portion of what it captures into the ground, releasing sugars and acids from its roots to feed the fungi and bacteria that supply it with nitrogen and phosphorus. Those microbes live briefly, die, and leave their bodies behind. Much of what ends up locked in soil for centuries passed through a microbe first; it is less the wreckage of leaves than the residue of the organisms that ate them.

Not all of that residue is equally secure. Some of it sits loose among the mineral grains as recognizable fragments, root hairs and scraps of leaf, and is consumed within a few years by whatever finds it. The rest binds chemically to particles of clay and silt, wrapping itself so closely around the mineral surface that enzymes cannot reach it. The loose fraction responds quickly to a warm summer or a wet spring; the bound fraction can persist for a thousand years, indifferent to weather, until the surface it clings to is disturbed.

That last condition is the one agriculture removes. A plough breaks the soil aggregates open and exposes surfaces that had been sealed for centuries; microbes reach what they could not reach before, and ground that had been a sink becomes, for a season or two, a source. Roughly half the carbon in the world's cultivated soils has left them by this route since farming began.

The reverse is possible but not symmetrical. Restoring cover crops and abandoning the plough will rebuild the loose fraction within a decade, which is why early measurements of such experiments look encouraging. The bound fraction returns only on the timescale that formed it. A field can be managed into looking recovered long before it has recovered, and the difference is invisible until the two fractions are separated in a laboratory.

The road ends at a gate, and past the gate the land goes flat and stays flat for a mile, until the flatness becomes water without ever having troubled to become a shore. This is the marsh at the mouth of our river. In August the cordgrass stands as high as my shoulder and the channels wander through it like cracks in old glaze. At low tide the banks lean back and show their gray sides, and the whole place smells of sulfur and cut grass, a smell that visitors find unpleasant for about ten minutes and then stop noticing.

I grew up half an hour inland, among hemlocks, and for years the marsh looked mean to me. A forest gives a child something to admire at once: height, shade, the sense of a room with a ceiling. The marsh gives nothing at once. It is a horizontal country, and what it withholds in the first minute it hands over in the fortieth, and only to someone willing to stand in one place long enough to be bitten.

What finally held me was the tide, which is not an event but a schedule. Twice a day the water walks in over the flats at the speed of a slow reader, and everything the marsh contains rearranges itself around that walking. The fiddler crabs come out in the hour after the water leaves and go down again before it returns. The heron works the edge of the falling water, because the edge is where the small fish lose their room. Even the grass sorts itself by inches of elevation, one species below and another above, a boundary no one could draw with a ruler and the plants redraw every year without discussion.

The hemlocks of my childhood changed too, of course, but at a pace no child could catch: a century of change in a lifetime of watching. The marsh changes in front of you, and changes back, and changes the same way again tomorrow. I have come to think that this is why I go.
